lines: This shop runs its own revenue-by-product pipeline two ways at once: a streaming job, and a separate nightly batch job.
For several days running, those two jobs genuinely disagreed on one single product, and nobody could actually say which number was the right one.
It turned out the batch job treated a refund issued right after midnight completely differently from how the streaming job treated that exact same refund.
A colleague now proposes tearing the whole batch layer out, going with pure streaming instead, no second path at all.
When is that genuinely the right call to make, and when does it quietly make the next restatement flatly impossible?
answer: A single code path obviously can't drift away from itself, sure, but it still carries a perfectly real reprocessing cost, and a perfectly real limit on how far back its own retained log actually reaches.
The right call here depends entirely on whether this pipeline's own numbers happen to fall under the thresholds that make pure streaming genuinely sufficient on its own.

lines: Design A, called Kappa, is one single streaming program running over a retained log, with replay as its only reprocessing path.
Design B, called Lambda, is a streaming speed layer plus a separate batch layer, merged together only at serve time.
Each one of these two designs gets its own estimate, its own failure table, and its own cost, computed independently.
Kappa's own cost to recompute a full year comes from replaying the entire retained log straight through the streaming engine itself.
Lambda's cost, by contrast, simply re-runs its own cheap batch layer directly over the lake instead.
Those two cost lines cross at one specific retention length and reprocessing frequency, computed directly from this shop's own real numbers.
The exact same synthetic stream now runs through both of these paths at once, with one single rule deliberately made to diverge between them: how a post-midnight refund actually gets treated.
The two resulting outputs get plotted right beside each other.
They diverge at exactly the one spot where that difference was deliberately planted, and nowhere else at all.
One single program, executed by one shared engine in either streaming mode or batch mode, produces genuinely matching results whenever its input happens to be bounded.
That's real, measurable progress toward solving this problem.
But it's still a second mode underneath, and that second mode still has to be kept correct, right alongside the first.
Four specifically named cases get checked directly against this shop's own actual numbers.

Billing-grade counts that must absorb genuinely very late data. Reprocessing that's simply too large or too slow for a streaming replay to handle. A logic change that needs a join against some huge historical dimension table. And a compliance-driven restatement.
A decision card lines all four of those named conditions up directly against this exact pipeline's own current numbers, checking each one in turn.
Whichever conditions actually end up met are what decide whether the batch layer stays in place.
No vague appeal to caution gets to stand in for an actual number here.
Two separate designs for the exact same pipeline, each one genuinely priced on its own terms.
A reprocessing-cost crossover, fully computed. A single planted edge case, measured as actual, real drift between the two paths.
A unified engine that genuinely helps here, without ever removing that second path entirely. And a batch-layer decision, stated plainly as four conditions anyone could go check.

One more, to use this for real: a pure Kappa pipeline now needs years of history fully recomputed, after a logic change that requires joining against a dimension table far larger than its own retained log's window.
What's genuinely the right move here?
answer: Simply extending the log's retention window to cover however many years are needed trades directly against both storage cost and streaming throughput, and a replay still flatly can't join against a dimension the log itself was never built to hold in the first place.
The huge-historical-dimension join is already one of the four named conditions that justify keeping a batch layer around, so this request maps directly onto a threshold that already exists.
